en: Udāna 3.10 Lokasutta Thus have I heard:
At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Uruvelā on the bank of the river Nerañjarā at the foot of the Bodhi tree, having just attained full enlightenment.
Now at that time, the Blessed One remained seated cross-legged for seven days experiencing the bliss of liberation.
Then, at the end of those seven days, the Blessed One arose from that concentration and surveyed the world with the eye of a Buddha.
As the Blessed One surveyed with the eye of a Buddha, he saw beings tormented by many fevers and burning with many fevers of passion,
hatred, and delusion.
Then the Blessed One, having understood this matter, on that occasion uttered this inspired exclamation:
“This world is born of anguish;
oppressed by contact, it calls disease ‘self.
For whatever it conceives of, [it suffers].”
Then it becomes otherwise. The world, subject to change, attached to existence,
and overcome by existence, delights only in existence.
What one delights in is fear;
what one fears is suffering.
Indeed, for the sake of abandoning existence—
This holy life is lived for the sake of this:
"Whatever ascetics or brahmins have claimed liberation from existence through further existence, I say they were all not liberated from existence.
And whatever ascetics or brahmins have claimed escape from existence through non-existence, I say they were all not escaped from existence."
For it is dependent on acquisitions that this suffering arises; with the destruction of all clinging, there is no arising of suffering.
Behold this world:
beings are overcome by manifold ignorance, delighting in existence, and are not yet liberated.
"Whatever states there may be, in any way or at any time— all those states are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change.
One who sees this thus as it really is with right wisdom—
Craving for existence is abandoned,
and one does not delight in non-existence;
through the total destruction of all cravings, [Nibbāna is realized].
The complete fading away and cessation [of lust] is Nibbāna.
For that monk who has attained extinction,
there is no further becoming through lack of clinging.
Māra has been overcome, the battle won;
such a one has transcended all states of existence.
Thus ends the tenth [verse].
The third chapter, the Nanda-vagga.
Its summary (uddāna) is:
Kamma, Nanda, and Yasoja.
Sāriputta and Kolita;
Pilindavaccha and Kassapa—
these ten are the skills by which they support the world.
